<reason>B won the central allocation clash. A answered the pressure questions directly and offered meaningful safeguards, but its public-care guarantee removed the immediate eviction advantage. B then explained why affordability limits do not themselves justify charging otherwise comparable adults differently because their parents become poor. A largely repeated reciprocity and “strangers first” without adequately answering progressive funding or distinguishing parental responsibility from a repayment obligation. Possible budget relief remained a benefit for A, but B more convincingly challenged the justification for this particular collection mechanism and its administrative burdens.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s question about uninterrupted care secured A’s commitment to public coverage during disputes. B then sharply distinguished protecting the parent from recovering costs: the eviction example could no longer establish why the child specifically should owe reimbursement. This narrowed the debate to the justification A defended least successfully.</best_rebuttal>
